A.q: Which set consists entirely of combining forms that mean skin?
A.explain: Derm/o, Dermat/o, and Cutane/o are the three interchangeable combining forms for skin, seen in dermal, dermatologist, and cutaneous. Cyt/o, Derm/o, and Cutane/o mixes in Cyt/o, which means cell. Dermat/o, Enter/o, and Hepat/o mixes in Enter/o (small intestine) and Hepat/o (liver). Cutane/o, Scler/o, and Sten/o mixes in Scler/o (hard) and Sten/o (narrow). Each wrong set therefore contains a form that names a cell, an organ, or a quality rather than skin.

A.q: Which two combining forms both mean poison?
A.explain: Tox/o and Toxic/o are the two spellings of the poison combining form, as in toxicoderma and cytotoxic. The other pairs are real combining forms from the same set but name different things: Carcin/o (cancer) and Necr/o (death), Lith/o (stone) and Sten/o (narrow), Crin/o (to secrete) and Phag/o (to eat or swallow).

A.q: Which combining form means cell?
A.explain: Cyt/o means cell, as in cytotoxic. Derm/o means skin, Enter/o means small intestine, and Hepat/o means liver.

A.q: Which combining form means small intestine?
A.explain: Enter/o means small intestine, as in enterocele. Esophag/o means esophagus, Gastr/o means stomach, and Hepat/o means liver.

A.q: Which combining form means esophagus?
A.explain: Esophag/o means esophagus, as in esophagoscopy. Enter/o means small intestine, Gastr/o means stomach, and Hepat/o means liver.

A.q: Which combining form means stomach?
A.explain: Gastr/o means stomach, as in gastroptosis. Enter/o means small intestine, Esophag/o means esophagus, and Hepat/o means liver.

A.q: Which combining form means liver?
A.explain: Hepat/o means liver, as in hepatectomy. Gastr/o means stomach, Enter/o means small intestine, and Esophag/o means esophagus.

A.q: Which combining form means cancer?
A.explain: Carcin/o means cancer, as in carcinoma. Necr/o means death, Onc/o means tumor or mass, and Path/o means disease.

A.q: Which combining form means to secrete?
A.explain: Crin/o means to secrete, as in endocrinology. Cyt/o means cell, Esthesi/o means sensation, and Fibr/o means fiber.

A.q: Which combining form means sensation?
A.explain: Esthesi/o means sensation, as in anesthesia. Crin/o means to secrete, Cyt/o means cell, and Gen/o means origin or production.

A.q: Which combining form means fiber?
A.explain: Fibr/o means fiber, as in fibroadenoma. Crin/o means to secrete, Esthesi/o means sensation, and Gen/o means origin or production.

A.q: Which combining form means origin or production?
A.explain: Gen/o means origin or production, as in genogram. Gynec/o means woman, Crin/o means to secrete, and Fibr/o means fiber.

A.q: Which combining form means woman?
A.explain: Gynec/o means woman, as in gynecologist. Gen/o means origin or production, Esthesi/o means sensation, and Crin/o means to secrete.

A.q: Which combining form means stone?
A.explain: Lith/o means stone, as in lithotripsy. Necr/o means death, Onc/o means tumor or mass, and Scler/o means hard.

A.q: Which combining form means death?
A.explain: Necr/o means death, as in necrosis. Lith/o means stone, Onc/o means tumor or mass, and Path/o means disease.

A.q: Which combining form means tumor or mass?
A.explain: Onc/o means tumor or mass, as in oncology. Necr/o means death, Carcin/o means cancer, and Path/o means disease.

A.q: Which combining form means straight, normal, or correct?
A.explain: Orth/o means straight, normal, or correct, as in orthopedist. Morph/o means form, Path/o means disease, and Phas/o means speech.

A.q: Which combining form means form?
A.explain: Morph/o means form, as in morphometry. Orth/o means straight or correct, Path/o means disease, and Phag/o means eat or swallow.

A.q: Which combining form means disease?
A.explain: Path/o means disease, as in pathobiologist. Phas/o means speech, Phag/o means eat or swallow, and Phob/o means exaggerated fear or sensitivity.

A.q: Which combining form carries two senses, child and foot?
A.explain: Ped/o carries two senses, child and foot, so the sense in any given term must be read from the rest of the word, as in bipedal where the prefix bi- for two points to the foot sense. Path/o means disease, Phag/o means eat or swallow, and Phas/o means speech.

A.q: Which combining form means eat or swallow?
A.explain: Phag/o means eat or swallow, as in phagophobia. Phas/o means speech, Path/o means disease, and Phob/o means exaggerated fear or sensitivity.

A.q: Which combining form means speech?
A.explain: Phas/o means speech, as in paraphasia. Phag/o means eat or swallow, Path/o means disease, and Phob/o means exaggerated fear or sensitivity.

A.q: Which combining form means exaggerated fear or sensitivity?
A.explain: Phob/o means exaggerated fear or sensitivity, as in hydrophobia and phagophobia. Phag/o means eat or swallow, Phas/o means speech, and Path/o means disease.

A.q: Which combining form means narrow?
A.explain: Sten/o means narrow, as in stenosis. Scler/o means hard, Son/o means sound, and Necr/o means death.

A.q: Which combining form means hard?
A.explain: Scler/o means hard, as in scleroderma. Sten/o means narrow, Son/o means sound, and Necr/o means death.

A.q: Which combining form means sound?
A.explain: Son/o means sound, as in sonographer. Sten/o means narrow, Scler/o means hard, and Necr/o means death.

A.q: All of the following pairs are synonym combining forms, that is, two spellings of the same meaning, EXCEPT:
A.explain: Cyt/o means cell and Gen/o means origin or production, so this pair is not a synonym set and is the exception. The other three pairs are alternate spellings of one meaning: Derm/o, Dermat/o, and Cutane/o all mean skin, and Tox/o and Toxic/o both mean poison.

A.q: Which combining form denotes a physiological function rather than a structure or a substance?
A.explain: Crin/o means to secrete, an action or function. Cyt/o (cell) and Hepat/o (liver) name structures, and Lith/o (stone) names a substance or formed mass, so the only function word among the choices is Crin/o.

A.q: All of the following combining forms are classed with the general or abstract group rather than with organs and structures EXCEPT:
A.explain: Hepat/o means liver and names an organ, so it is the exception. Lith/o (stone), Necr/o (death), and Onc/o (tumor or mass) belong to the general or abstract group, denoting a thing or a process rather than an organ.

A.q: In the term lithotripsy (CF+S), the element -tripsy refers to which action?
A.explain: The element -tripsy means crushing, so lithotripsy is the crushing of stones. The stone sense in the same word comes from the combining form Lith/o, not from -tripsy; secreting is Crin/o and speech is Phas/o, neither of which is present here.

A.q: In the term hydrophobia (CF+R+S), the element hydr refers to what?
A.explain: Hydr means water, so hydrophobia is an exaggerated fear of or sensitivity to water. The fear sense in the same word is carried by the root phob, while cell is Cyt/o and stone is Lith/o; attributing water to phob or fear to hydr would swap the two parts of the term.

A.q: In the term fibroadenoma (CF+R+S), the element aden refers to what?
A.explain: Aden means gland, so the aden element names the glandular tissue in fibroadenoma. The fiber sense in the same word comes from Fibr/o and the tumor sense from the suffix -oma, while skin is Derm/o; a fibroadenoma is a benign tumor built of fibrous and glandular tissue, so fiber, gland, and tumor each map to a different part.

A.q: In the term pathobiologist (CF+CF+S), the element bi refers to what?
A.explain: Bi means life, so the bi element contributes the sense of living processes in pathobiologist. The disease sense in the same word comes from Path/o and the specialist sense from the suffix -logist, while form is Morph/o; a pathobiologist is one who specializes in the study of the life and nature of disease.

A.q: The combining form Ped/o carries two senses, child and foot. In the term bipedal (P+R+S), which sense applies?
A.explain: In bipedal the prefix bi- means two, so the structure counted is feet, and ped takes the foot sense, giving having two feet. The child sense of Ped/o is the other reading and is the natural mispick here, while cell is Cyt/o and stomach is Gastr/o; the dual gloss of Ped/o means the sense must be chosen from the rest of the word, and two of something points to feet.

A.q: In the term scleroderma (CF+R), the element scler refers to what?
A.explain: Scler means hard, so scleroderma is a hardening of the skin, with derma as the root for skin. Narrow is Sten/o, sound is Son/o, and stone is Lith/o; reading scler as narrow or sound would swap it with a different quality form.

A.q: What does the term cytotoxic mean?
A.explain: Cytotoxic is built from Cyt/o (cell) and tox (poison) with -ic (pertaining to), so it means damaging or poisonous to cells. Pertaining to the skin would use Derm/o or Cutane/o, pertaining to the small intestine would use Enter/o, and pertaining to the liver would use Hepat/o.

A.q: What does the term dermatologist mean?
options: A specialist in disorders of the skin
A technician who records skin images
A surgeon who repairs the skin after burns
A specialist in disorders of the hair only
A.explain: Dermatologist is built from Dermat/o (skin) and -ologist (specialist), so it denotes a specialist in disorders of the skin. The other options keep part of the term but change another word part, so they do not match.

A.q: What does the term enterocele mean?
options: A hernia of the small intestine
A.explain: Enterocele is built from Enter/o (small intestine) and -cele (hernia), so it denotes a hernia of the small intestine. Downward displacement of the stomach is gastroptosis, examining the esophagus is esophagoscopy, and removal of the liver is hepatectomy.

A.q: What does the term esophagoscopy mean?
options: Process of examining the esophagus with an instrument
Surgical removal of part or all of the esophagus
Downward displacement or drooping of the esophagus
A hernia of the esophagus through a weakness
A.explain: Esophagoscopy is Esophag/o (esophagus) plus -scopy (process of examining with an instrument). Removal would be -ectomy, drooping would be -ptosis, and a hernia would be -cele.

A.q: What does the term gastroptosis mean?
options: Downward displacement or drooping of the stomach
Inflammation of the lining of the stomach
A hernia of the stomach through the diaphragm
Surgical removal of part of the stomach
A.explain: Gastroptosis is built from Gastr/o (stomach) and -ptosis (downward displacement or drooping), so it denotes a drooping of the stomach. The other options keep part of the term but change another word part, so they do not match.

A.q: What does the term hepatectomy mean?
A.explain: Hepatectomy is built from Hepat/o (liver) and -ectomy (surgical removal), so it denotes surgical removal of the liver. The other options keep part of the term but change another word part, so they do not match.

A.q: What does the term carcinoma mean?
options: A benign tumor of glandular tissue
A.explain: Carcinoma is built from Carcin/o (cancer) and -oma (tumor), so it denotes a malignant, cancerous tumor. The vowel-initial -oma drops the combining vowel o, so the form is R+S. A benign glandular tumor is fibroadenoma, the study of tumors is oncology, and tissue death is necrosis.

A.q: What does the term endocrinology mean?
options: The study of glands and the substances they secrete within
Loss of sensation produced by blocking ordinary sensory input
A written record of origin or of family relationships
A clinical specialist in disorders that affect women
A.explain: Endocrinology is built from endo- (within), Crin/o (to secrete), and -logy (study), so it denotes the study of glands and the substances they secrete within the body. Loss of sensation is anesthesia, a record of origin is genogram, and a specialist in disorders of women is gynecologist.

A.q: What does the term anesthesia mean?
options: The study of glands and their secretions
A.explain: Anesthesia is built from an- (without), Esthesi/o (sensation), and -ia (condition), so it denotes loss of sensation. The vowel-initial -ia leaves the root bare, so the form is P+R+S. The study of glands is endocrinology, fear of water is hydrophobia, and hardening of the skin is scleroderma.

A.q: What does the term fibroadenoma mean?
options: A benign tumor composed of fibrous and glandular tissue
A malignant tumor composed of fibrous and glandular tissue
A benign tumor composed of fatty and glandular tissue
A benign tumor composed of fibrous and muscle tissue
A.explain: Fibroadenoma is Fibr/o (fiber) plus Aden/o (gland) plus -oma (tumor), a benign tumor of fibrous and glandular tissue. It is not malignant, and it contains neither fat nor muscle.

A.q: What does the term genogram mean?
options: A record of origin or of family relationships
The study of tumors and other abnormal masses
The process of measuring form or body shape
A condition of death in tissue or in cells
A.explain: Genogram is built from Gen/o (origin or production) and -gram (record), so it denotes a record of origin or of family relationships. The study of tumors is oncology, measuring form is morphometry, and tissue death is necrosis.

A.q: What does the term gynecologist mean?
options: A specialist in disorders of women
A specialist in disorders of the skin
A specialist who studies the nature of disease
A specialist who performs imaging using sound waves
A.explain: Gynecologist is built from Gynec/o (woman) and -ologist (specialist), so it denotes a specialist in disorders of women. A skin specialist is dermatologist, a specialist in the nature of disease is pathobiologist, and a sound-imaging specialist is sonographer.

A.q: What does the term lithotripsy mean?
options: Crushing of a stone or of stones
A benign tumor of fiber and gland tissue
Abnormal narrowing of a passage or vessel
Hardening of the skin over a body region
A.explain: Lithotripsy is built from Lith/o (stone) and -tripsy (crushing), so it denotes crushing of stones. A benign glandular tumor is fibroadenoma, abnormal narrowing is stenosis, and hardening of the skin is scleroderma.

A.q: What does the term necrosis mean?
options: Death of tissue or of cells
The study of tumors or masses
A.explain: Necrosis is built from Necr/o (death) and -osis (condition), so it denotes death of tissue or cells. The study of tumors is oncology, hardening of the skin is scleroderma, and abnormal narrowing is stenosis.

A.q: What does the term oncology mean?
A.explain: Oncology is built from Onc/o (tumor or mass) and -logy (study), so it denotes the study of tumors. Tissue death is necrosis, a benign glandular tumor is fibroadenoma, and a malignant pigment tumor is melanoma.

A.q: What does the term orthopedist mean?
options: A specialist in the correction of musculoskeletal deformities
A specialist who studies the life and nature of disease
A specialist in disorders that specifically affect women
A specialist in disorders that specifically affect the skin
A.explain: Orthopedist is built from Orth/o (straight or correct), ped (child or foot), and -ist (specialist), so it denotes a specialist in the correction of deformities of the musculoskeletal structure. A specialist in the nature of disease is pathobiologist, a specialist in women is gynecologist, and a skin specialist is dermatologist.

A.q: What does the term morphometry mean?
options: A record of origin or of family relationships
A.explain: Morphometry is built from Morph/o (form) and -metry (measurement), so it denotes the process of measuring form. The study of tumors is oncology, a record of origin is genogram, and tissue death is necrosis.

A.q: What does the term pathobiologist mean?
options: A specialist who studies the nature of disease
A specialist in disorders of women
A specialist in disorders of the skin
A specialist in the correction of musculoskeletal deformities
A.explain: Pathobiologist is built from Path/o (disease), bi/o (life), and -logist (specialist), so it denotes a specialist who studies the nature of disease, with two roots giving CF+CF+S. A specialist in women is gynecologist, a skin specialist is dermatologist, and a musculoskeletal specialist is orthopedist.

A.q: What does the term phagophobia mean?
options: Exaggerated fear of eating or swallowing
Exaggerated fear of or sensitivity to water
A disorder featuring errors of speech
A skin condition caused by poison
A.explain: Phagophobia is built from Phag/o (eat or swallow), phob (fear), and -ia (condition), so it denotes an exaggerated fear of eating or swallowing. Fear of water is hydrophobia, errors of speech is paraphasia, and a poison skin condition is toxicoderma.

A.q: What does the term paraphasia mean?
options: A disorder featuring errors of speech
Exaggerated fear of eating or swallowing
A skin condition caused by poison
A.explain: Paraphasia is built from para- (abnormal), Phas/o (speech), and -ia (condition), so it denotes a disorder featuring errors of speech. Fear of eating is phagophobia, a poison skin condition is toxicoderma, and hardening of the skin is scleroderma.

A.q: What does the term toxicoderma mean?
options: A skin condition caused by poison
A disorder featuring errors of speech
A.explain: Toxicoderma is built from Toxic/o (poison) and derma (skin), so it denotes a skin condition caused by poison, with derma as a root giving CF+R. Hardening of the skin is scleroderma, fear of water is hydrophobia, and speech errors is paraphasia.

A.q: What does the term hydrophobia mean?
options: Exaggerated fear of or sensitivity to water
Exaggerated fear of eating or of swallowing
A skin condition caused by exposure to poison
Loss of sensation affecting a body region
A.explain: Hydrophobia is built from Hydr/o (water), phob (fear), and -ia (condition), so it denotes an exaggerated fear of or sensitivity to water. Fear of eating is phagophobia, a poison skin condition is toxicoderma, and loss of sensation is anesthesia.

A.q: What does the term stenosis mean?
options: Abnormal narrowing of a passage or vessel
A record of origin or of family relationships
A.explain: Stenosis is built from Sten/o (narrow) and -osis (condition), so it denotes an abnormal narrowing of a passage or vessel. The root sten ends in a consonant and the vowel-initial -osis drops the combining vowel, giving R+S. Hardening of the skin is scleroderma, tissue death is necrosis, and a record of origin is genogram.

A.q: What does the term scleroderma mean?
options: A skin condition caused by poison
A.explain: Scleroderma is built from Scler/o (hard) and derma (skin), so it denotes hardening of the skin, with derma as a root giving CF+R. Abnormal narrowing is stenosis, a poison skin condition is toxicoderma, and fear of water is hydrophobia.

A.q: What does the term sonographer mean?
options: A specialist who performs imaging using sound waves
A specialist who treats hearing loss from loud sound
A device that records sound waves from the heart
A specialist who studies the physics of sound
A.explain: Sonographer is built from Son/o (sound) and -grapher (one who records or images), so it denotes a specialist who performs imaging using sound waves. The other options keep part of the term but change another word part, so they do not match.

A.q: Hepatectomy is built as R+S while gastroptosis is built as CF+S, although both join an organ combining form to a surgical suffix. Which statement explains the difference?
options: The suffix -ptosis begins with a vowel, so o is dropped; the suffix -ectomy begins with a consonant, so the combining vowel o is kept.
Both suffixes begin with consonants, but -ectomy drops the combining vowel under a same-vowel rule at the join.
Both terms keep the combining vowel o, but hepatectomy hides it because the root hepat itself ends in a vowel.
The suffix -ectomy begins with a vowel, so o is dropped; the suffix -ptosis begins with a consonant, so the combining vowel o is kept.
A.explain: A consonant-final root plus a vowel-initial suffix takes no combining vowel, whereas a consonant-final root plus a consonant-initial suffix keeps the combining vowel o. The root hepat ends in a consonant and -ectomy opens with the vowel e, so no o appears and the form is R+S (hepat + ectomy). The root gastr ends in a consonant and -ptosis opens with the consonant p, so o is inserted and the form is CF+S (gastr/o + ptosis). Reversing which suffix is vowel-initial swaps the two builds. A same-vowel drop needs identical vowels meeting at the join, which neither term has. Tying the drop to a vowel at the end of hepat is wrong, because hepat ends in a consonant.

A.q: Carcinoma is built as R+S while oncology is built as CF+S, although both are built on a combining form for an abnormal growth. Which statement explains the difference?
options: The suffix -logy begins with a vowel, so o is dropped; the suffix -oma begins with a consonant, so the combining vowel o is kept.
The suffix -oma begins with a vowel, so o is dropped; the suffix -logy begins with a consonant, so the combining vowel o is kept.
Both suffixes begin with consonants, but -oma drops the combining vowel under a same-vowel rule at the join.
Both terms keep the combining vowel o, but carcinoma hides it because the root carcin itself ends in a vowel.
A.explain: The root carcin ends in a consonant and the suffix -oma opens with the vowel o, so no combining vowel is used and the form is R+S (carcin + oma). The root onc ends in a consonant and the suffix -logy opens with the consonant l, so the combining vowel o is kept and the form is CF+S (onc/o + logy). Reversing which suffix is vowel-initial swaps the two builds. A same-vowel drop needs identical vowels meeting at the join, which neither term has. Tying the drop to a vowel at the end of carcin is wrong, because carcin ends in a consonant.

A.q: Dermal and cutaneous are built as R+S while dermatologist is built as CF+S, although all three use a combining form for skin. Which statement explains the difference?
options: The suffix -logist begins with a vowel, so dermatologist drops o, while -al and -ous begin with consonants and should keep the combining vowel
Both -al and -ous begin with consonants, so dermal and cutaneous should keep o, and -logist drops it by a same-vowel rule
The suffixes -al and -ous begin with vowels, so o is dropped (R+S); the suffix -logist begins with a consonant, so o is kept (CF+S)
All three terms keep the combining vowel o, but dermal and cutaneous lose it because derm and cutane end in a vowel
A.explain: The roots derm and cutane end in consonants and the suffixes -al and -ous open with vowels, so no combining vowel is used and the forms are R+S (derm + al, cutane + ous). Dermatologist is analyzed as dermat/o + logist: the suffix -logist opens with the consonant l, so the combining vowel o is kept and the form is CF+S. Treating -logist as vowel-initial would drop o and contradict that build. Treating -al and -ous as consonant-initial would keep o in dermal and cutaneous, which the builds do not. Tying the drop to a vowel at the end of derm or cutane is wrong, because both roots end in a consonant.

A.q: Anesthesia is built as P+R+S while endocrinology is built as P+CF+S, although both place a prefix before a combining form. Which statement explains the difference at the root-suffix join?
options: The suffix -ia begins with a vowel, so aesthesi stands bare (R); -logy begins with a consonant, so crin keeps combining vowel o (CF)
The suffix -logy begins with a vowel, so crin stands bare; the suffix -ia begins with a consonant, so aesthesi keeps combining vowel o
Both suffixes begin with consonants, but -ia drops the combining vowel under a same-vowel rule that these two joins do not meet
The difference comes from the prefixes: an- ends in a consonant so no vowel is added, while endo- ends in a vowel so o is inserted
A.explain: After the prefix, the build is decided by the root-suffix join. In anesthesia the root aesthesi meets the vowel-initial suffix -ia, so no combining vowel is used and the root is bare, giving P+R+S. In endocrinology the root crin meets the consonant-initial suffix -logy, so the combining vowel o is kept, giving P+CF+S. The prefix endo- ends in a vowel, but the root crin begins with a consonant, so the prefix-vowel rule is not triggered and endo- keeps its o. Reversing the suffix initials swaps the two builds. A same-vowel drop needs identical vowels meeting at the join, which neither term has. Attributing the difference to the prefixes misses the join that actually decides R versus CF.

A.q: Fibroadenoma is built as CF+R+S. The combining vowel o after fibr is retained even though the next element aden begins with the vowel a. Which principle accounts for this?
options: The o is dropped in correct spelling, so the build should be recorded as R+R+S rather than as CF+R+S.
The o links two roots, and a combining vowel bridges roots even when the next root opens with a vowel; the drop applies at a suffix.
The o is kept because the closing suffix -oma begins with a vowel, and that vowel forces a combining vowel earlier in the word.
The o is kept because a prefix fib- ends in a consonant, and a consonant-final prefix inserts a combining vowel after itself.
A.explain: Fibroadenoma stacks two roots, fibr (fiber) and aden (gland), before the suffix -oma. Where two roots are joined, a combining vowel o is inserted to bridge them, and this holds even when the following root opens with a vowel. The drop-before-a-vowel behavior belongs to a root meeting a vowel-initial suffix, not to a root meeting another root. Hence fibr/o is a combining form, aden is the bare root, and -oma is the suffix, giving CF+R+S. Deleting the bridge would mis-analyze the word. The retention is not caused by the suffix -oma. There is no prefix fib- in the term.

A.q: Toxicoderma is built as CF+R while cytotoxic is built as CF+R+S. What explains that one term has no suffix?
options: Cytotoxic has no suffix, because the ending -ic is a combining vowel and not a word part with its own meaning.
Toxicoderma has no suffix, because derma is a root meaning skin: a combining form plus a root, then it stops.
Both terms have a suffix, but the suffix in toxicoderma is silent and is not written in the finished word.
Toxicoderma loses a suffix under the same-vowel rule, which deletes a whole ending when two vowels meet.
A.explain: In toxicoderma the element derma is a root (skin), not a suffix, so the word is the combining form tox/o plus the root derma with no closing suffix, giving CF+R. In cytotoxic the element -ic is a true suffix (pertaining to) attached after the root tox, giving CF+R+S. Calling -ic a combining vowel mislabels a suffix. There is no silent suffix in toxicoderma. The same-vowel rule drops a combining vowel at a join and does not delete a whole suffix.

A.q: Cutaneous is built as R+S while sonographer is built as CF+S. Which statement explains the difference at the root-suffix join?
options: The suffix -ous begins with a vowel, so cutane stands bare (R); -grapher begins with a consonant, so son keeps its combining vowel o (CF)
The element -grapher begins with a vowel, so son stands bare; the suffix -ous begins with a consonant, so cutane keeps its combining vowel o
Both elements begin with consonants, but -ous drops the combining vowel under a same-vowel rule that this join does not meet
Both terms keep the combining vowel o, but cutaneous loses it because the root cutane is analyzed as ending in a vowel
A.explain: The root cutane ends in a consonant and the suffix -ous opens with the vowel o, so no combining vowel is used and the form is R+S (cutane + ous). The root son ends in a consonant and the element -grapher opens with the consonant g, so the combining vowel o is kept, giving CF+S (son/o + grapher). Reversing the initial letters swaps the two builds. A same-vowel drop needs identical vowels meeting at the join, which neither term has. Tying the drop to a vowel at the end of cutane is wrong, because cutane ends in a consonant.

A.q: Match each organ or structure combining form to the meaning it conveys.
A.explain: Cyt/o means cell, as in cytotoxic. Derm/o means skin, as in dermal. Enter/o means small intestine, as in enterocele. Esophag/o means esophagus, as in esophagoscopy. Gastr/o means stomach, as in gastroptosis. Hepat/o means liver, as in hepatectomy. These six forms name organs or structures, and each pairs with exactly one meaning.

A.q: Match each remaining combining form from the general group to the meaning it conveys.
A.explain: Carcin/o means cancer, as in carcinoma. Crin/o means to secrete, as in endocrinology. Esthesi/o means sensation, as in anesthesia. Fibr/o means fiber, as in fibroadenoma. Gen/o means origin or production, as in genogram. Gynec/o means woman, as in gynecologist. These six forms belong to the general or abstract group, and each pairs with exactly one meaning.

A.q: Match each remaining combining form to the meaning it conveys.
A.explain: Lith/o means stone, as in lithotripsy. Necr/o means death, as in necrosis. Onc/o means tumor or mass, as in oncology. Orth/o means straight, normal, or correct, as in orthopedist. Morph/o means form, as in morphometry. Path/o means disease, as in pathobiologist. Each form pairs with exactly one meaning.

A.q: Match each remaining combining form, including the poison pair, to the meaning it conveys.
A.explain: Ped/o means child or foot, as in bipedal where the prefix points to the foot. Phag/o means eat or swallow, as in phagophobia. Phas/o means speech, as in paraphasia. Tox/o and Toxic/o both mean poison, as in toxicoderma. Phob/o means exaggerated fear or sensitivity, as in hydrophobia. Sten/o means narrow, as in stenosis. Note that Ped/o alone carries two senses, and Tox/o and Toxic/o are two spellings of one meaning.

A.q: Match each built term to the word-part pattern used to form it.
A.explain: Cytotoxic joins Cyt/o, the root tox, and -ic, so the pattern is CF+R+S. Enterocele joins Enter/o and -cele, so the pattern is CF+S. Hepatectomy joins hepat and vowel-initial -ectomy with no combining vowel, so the pattern is R+S. Anesthesia joins an-, bare aesthesi, and vowel-initial -ia, so the pattern is P+R+S. Toxicoderma joins tox/o and the root derma with no suffix, so the pattern is CF+R. Endocrinology joins endo-, Crin/o, and -logy, so the pattern is P+CF+S. P+S fits none of these terms: each one has a root or a combining form between the prefix, if any, and the ending.

A.q: Which word-part pattern builds the term lithotripsy?
options: A root joined to a root
A root joined to a suffix
A prefix joined to a suffix
A.explain: Lithotripsy joins Lith/o (stone) to -tripsy (crushing). The suffix begins with a consonant, so the combining vowel o is kept and the pattern is a combining form plus a suffix (CF+S). A root joined to a root would need another root and no suffix. A root joined to a suffix would drop the combining vowel, which this consonant-initial suffix does not do. A prefix joined to a suffix would need a prefix and no stone root.

A.q: In endocrinology, the prefix endo- and the combining form crin/o mean which pair?
options: Outside the body, and a tumor
Within the body, and to secrete
In the middle, and to secrete
Above a structure, and a layer
A.explain: Endo- means within and Crin/o means to secrete, so endocrinology is the study of secretion within the body. Outside the body with a tumor swaps the prefix for its opposite and swaps secrete for a mass sense carried by Onc/o. In the middle keeps a location sense but not the within sense of endo-. Above a structure and a layer names neither the prefix nor the combining form in this term.

A.q: Which word part in hypoesthesia carries the meaning sensation?
A.explain: Hypoesthesia places hypo- (deficient or below) before the root esthesi (sensation) and the suffix -ia (condition), so the sensation sense is carried by esthesi, the root of Esthesi/o. The prefix hypo- names the degree, not the sensation. The suffix -ia names the condition, not the sensation. The prefix an- means without and appears in anesthesia, not in hypoesthesia.

A.q: Toxemia names a blood condition that involves which of the following?
A.explain: Toxemia joins tox (poison), the root of Tox/o and Toxic/o, to -emia (a blood condition), so it denotes poison in the blood. Formation of blood would use a production suffix such as -poiesis, not tox. Reduction of volume is not the sense of tox. Secretion is the sense of Crin/o, which this term does not contain.

A.q: Orthopedic joins orth/o and ped/o. Which pair of meanings do those forms contribute in that term?
options: A joint sense, and a baby
A.explain: Orth/o means straight, normal, or correct, and ped/o means child or foot. In orthopedic those forms are read as correct and foot, the pairing used for correction of the musculoskeletal structure, the same pairing as in orthopedist. A joint sense and a baby assigns neither form its taught sense. A muscle sense and foot keeps the foot sense of ped/o but replaces orth/o with a muscle sense it does not have. Straight alone and muscle keeps a true sense of orth/o but replaces the foot sense of ped/o with muscle.

A.q: Which build is genogram?
A.explain: Genogram joins Gen/o (origin or production) to the root gram (record). Gram is not a suffix, so no further ending is attached and the build is CF+R. CF+S would need a suffix after the combining form. R+S would drop the combining vowel, which this term keeps. P+CF+S would need a prefix, which genogram does not have.

A.q: Which build is orthopedist?
A.explain: Orthopedist joins Orth/o (straight or correct), the root ped (child or foot), and -ist (specialist), so the build is CF+R+S. CF+S would skip the ped root. R+S would drop the combining vowel before ped, which this term keeps. P+R+S would need a prefix, which orthopedist does not have.

A.q: Which pair of builds matches scleroderma, then stenosis?
A.explain: Scleroderma joins Scler/o to the root derma and has no suffix, so it is CF+R. Stenosis joins sten to vowel-initial -osis and drops the combining vowel, so it is R+S. R+S then CF+R reverses the two terms. CF+S then R+S treats scleroderma as if derma were a suffix. CF+R then CF+S keeps scleroderma right but treats -osis as consonant-initial.

A.q: Which build is hydrophobia?
A.explain: Hydrophobia joins Hydr/o (water), the root phob (fear), and -ia (condition), so the build is CF+R+S. CF+S would skip the phob root. R+S would drop the combining vowel before phob, which this term keeps. P+R+S would need a prefix, which hydrophobia does not have.

A.q: In the term cutaneous, what does Cutane/o stand for?
A.explain: Cutane/o means skin, so in cutaneous it is the skin element. The suffix -ous begins with a vowel, so the combining vowel is dropped and the written word is cutane + ous, still from Cutane/o. Hard is Scler/o, cell is Cyt/o, and poison is Tox/o or Toxic/o.
